title: People and how they seem
theme: talking about people: informal words and describing adjectives
goal: Recognise and use 22 high-frequency words for talking about people and describing them, in casual and polite speech.

items.en: guy, fellow (informal, very common in Québec)

example.fr: Karim, c'est un bon gars.
example.en: Karim is a good guy.

items.note: **Informal.** The r and the s are silent: [ga]. In Québec, *les gars* also means “guys” for a group of men.

example.fr: Il y a un mec qui t'attend dehors.
example.en: There's a guy waiting for you outside.

items.note: **Informal**, but not rude. *Mon mec* can mean “my boyfriend” in France.

example.fr: Je vais au cinéma avec des potes.
example.en: I'm going to the movies with some buddies.

items.note: **Informal.** Same form for a woman: *une pote*. In Québec you also hear *un chum* (a friend, or a boyfriend).

example.fr: Quand j'étais gamin, j'habitais à Moncton.
example.en: When I was a kid, I lived in Moncton.

items.note: **Informal.** Feminine: *une gamine*. In Québec, don't use the French slang word *gosse* for a child: there it is vulgar. Say *un enfant* or *un jeune*.

items.en: darling, honey (to a partner or child)

example.fr: Tu viens, ma chérie ? On est en retard.
example.en: Are you coming, honey? We're late.

example.fr: Pardon, mademoiselle, vous avez oublié votre sac.
example.en: Excuse me, miss, you forgot your bag.

items.note: Official forms no longer use it. *Madame* is the safe choice for any adult woman.

example.fr: L'erreur est humaine.
example.en: To err is human.

items.note: A person is *un être humain* (a human being).

example.fr: Ma voisine est américaine, elle vient de Boston.
example.en: My neighbour is American; she's from Boston.

items.note: No capital letter for the adjective. The people: *les Américains*.

example.fr: Ce n'est pas ton parapluie, c'est le mien.
example.en: That's not your umbrella, it's mine.

items.note: It agrees with the thing owned: *la mienne* (f.), *les miens*, *les miennes*. Also *le tien* (yours, friend), *le sien* (his/hers).

example.fr: Tu es fou ? Il fait moins trente dehors !
example.en: Are you crazy? It's minus thirty outside!

items.note: *Être fou de* = to be crazy about: *Elle est folle de hockey.*

example.fr: C'est dingue, il neige en mai !
example.en: It's unbelievable, it's snowing in May!

items.note: **Informal.** Same form for men and women. *C'est dingue !* = That's crazy!

example.fr: Ce n'est pas une question stupide.
example.en: It's not a stupid question.

example.fr: Je me sens idiot, j'ai raté le bus.
example.en: I feel like an idiot, I missed the bus.

example.fr: C'est bête, j'ai oublié mes clés.
example.en: How silly, I forgot my keys.

items.note: As a noun, *une bête* is an animal. In Québec, *être bête avec quelqu'un* means to be rude to them.

example.fr: Pourquoi tu es méchant avec ta sœur ?
example.en: Why are you mean to your sister?

items.note: On a gate: *Chien méchant* = Beware of the dog. In Québec, *un méchant party* = one heck of a party.

example.fr: Je me sens coupable de partir si tôt.
example.en: I feel guilty about leaving so early.

example.fr: Ton chat est trop mignon !
example.en: Your cat is so cute!

items.note: In Québec, *cute* itself is also used in casual speech.

example.fr: Il est marrant, ton frère.
example.en: Your brother is funny.

example.fr: Il a fait un temps horrible toute la semaine.
example.en: The weather was awful all week.

example.fr: Nous avons passé une soirée merveilleuse.
example.en: We had a wonderful evening.

example.fr: La vue sur le fleuve est fantastique.
example.en: The view of the river is fantastic.

items.en: sacred; (before a noun) a real, one heck of a

example.fr: C'est un sacré problème.
example.en: That's one heck of a problem.

items.note: In Québec, *sacrer* means “to swear”, and *les sacres* are swear words.

blocks.title: Register matters
blocks.body: [[gars]], [[mec]], [[pote]], [[gamin]], [[dingue]] and [[marrant]] are **informal**: fine with friends, not in a job interview. In Québec, [[gars]] is everywhere, while [[mec]] sounds French. [[Bête]] means *silly*, but in Québec [[être bête avec quelqu'un]] also means *to be rude to someone*. Watch the feminine: [[fou]] → [[folle]].

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Repeat each line out loud, then record yourself and compare.

lines.tip: gars sounds like “ga”: the r and the s are silent.

lines.fr: C'est bête, j'ai oublié mes clés.
lines.en: How silly, I forgot my keys.

lines.tip: mignon: gn sounds like the ny in “canyon”.

lines.en: I feel guilty about leaving so early.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.intro: Answer without scrolling back. Getting something wrong now helps you remember it later.

blocks.prompt: Match the casual words to their meaning.
Sofia's new puppy is tiny and adorable. What do you say?
You're writing to a woman you don't know at your bank. Which form of address is the safe choice?
blocks.explain: [[Madame]] is right for any adult woman. [[Mademoiselle]] is old-fashioned and no longer used on official forms.
optionFeedback: Mademoiselle is old-fashioned and can sound patronizing.
Ma chérie is for a partner or a child.

blocks.explain: The feminine of [[fou]] is [[folle]]; “crazy about” is [[fou de]].

blocks.prompt: It's not my bag, it's yours. (to a friend)
accept: Ce n'est pas mon sac, c'est le tien.
C'est pas mon sac, c'est le tien.
blocks.explain: [[Sac]] is masculine, so “yours” (to a friend) is [[le tien]].

blocks.text: Ce n'est pas ta valise, c'est la ___.
blocks.en: It's not your suitcase, it's mine.

blocks.text: Je me sens ___ : j'ai oublié l'anniversaire de Mei.
blocks.en: I feel guilty: I forgot Mei's birthday.

blocks.explain: [[sacré]] has an acute accent on the e.

blocks.prompt: What does the speaker say about the brother?
blocks.explain: [[marrant]] is a casual word for funny.

summary:
- Talk about people casually: [[gars, mec, pote, gamin]], and politely: [[mademoiselle]], [[mon chéri / ma chérie]]
- Describe people and things: [[fou, bête, méchant, mignon, marrant, merveilleux, horrible]]
- Say “mine” with [[le mien / la mienne]]
- Know which words are informal, and which to avoid in a formal setting
